title: Chapter 12 — Cooking: Ranges and Cooktops
intro: Gas, electric, and induction — the fuel conversation and the demo that converts.

sections.title: The Fuel Conversation
content: Every cooking sale starts with fuel. This is the first question you ask after 'What are you replacing?' The customer's answer determines your entire product set.

**Gas.** Open flame, instant visual heat, responsive temperature control. Preferred by customers who cook frequently and want to see and control the flame. Gas burners are measured in BTU — higher BTU means more heat output. A standard burner is 9,000–12,000 BTU. A power burner is 15,000–22,000 BTU. Pro-style ranges go to 25,000 BTU. Gas requires a gas line — if the customer doesn't have one, you're looking at a $500–$2,000 installation cost to run a line.

**Electric.** Smooth glass-ceramic cooktop with radiant elements underneath. Clean look, easy to wipe, flat surface doubles as counter space when not cooking. Heat is slower to respond than gas — there's lag between adjusting the dial and the surface changing temperature. Electric coil (budget, exposed elements) is nearly extinct in new kitchens. Electric requires a 240V outlet — most kitchens have one, but verify.

**Induction.** Uses electromagnetic energy to heat the pan directly — the cooktop surface stays relatively cool. Fastest boil time of any cooking technology. Precise temperature control. Requires induction-compatible cookware (magnetic — cast iron, most stainless steel, not aluminum or copper). This is the technology that converts customers on the floor — ALWAYS demo induction with the boil test. Put water on an induction burner and a gas burner simultaneously. Induction wins by minutes. The customer's eyes go wide. That's your close.

**Dual Fuel.** Gas cooktop on top, electric oven below. The best of both worlds — flame cooking with precise electric baking. This is the configuration most serious home cooks prefer. Premium price point. Available in 30", 36", and 48" widths. Wolf, Thermador, KitchenAid, JennAir, Miele, Monogram, and Café all offer dual fuel.

sections.title: Range Types and Configurations
content: **Freestanding Range.** Finished on all sides, backguard with controls on top. Can stand alone or slide between cabinets. Most affordable, most common. 30" standard width. This is what most customers are replacing.

**Slide-In Range.** No backguard — controls on the front. Designed to sit between countertops for a built-in look. Overlapping edges rest on the counter. More expensive than freestanding but dramatically better looking. This is the single most impactful upsell in cooking — the visual difference between a freestanding and slide-in is immediately obvious on the floor.
**Drop-In Range.** Sits into a cabinet cutout, supported by a base cabinet. Rare in new construction but common in replacement scenarios for older kitchens designed for drop-ins.

**Pro-Style Range.** Commercial-inspired aesthetic — heavy grates, large knobs, powerful burners, stainless steel construction. Available in 30", 36", 48", and 60" widths. Gas, dual fuel, or all-electric. Brands: Wolf, Thermador, JennAir RISE, Monogram, BlueStar, Viking, Bertazzoni, Miele, Café, La Cornue, AGA Mercury. Price: $3,500–$20,000+. The customer buying a pro-style range is building a kitchen around the range.

**Rangetop.** A cooktop that sits on a base cabinet — like the top half of a pro-style range. Paired with wall ovens. This is the configuration for customers who want maximum cooking surface AND maximum oven capacity. Common in luxury and serious-cook kitchens.

sections.title: Wall Ovens: Types That Matter
content: **Single Wall Oven.** 27" or 30" built into cabinetry at eye level. Convection is standard at mid-tier and above. True European convection (rear fan with heating element) is better than standard convection (bottom element with fan). Every major brand offers single wall ovens from $1,200 to $6,000+.

**Double Wall Oven.** Two ovens stacked. Essential for customers who entertain, cook holiday meals, or bake frequently. The question is whether they need two FULL ovens or one full + one smaller. Some brands offer combination units with a full oven and a smaller speed oven on top.

**Steam Oven.** Uses steam to cook — healthier (no oil needed), preserves nutrients, keeps food moist. Can steam vegetables, fish, bread, reheat leftovers without drying them out. Miele, Thermador, Bosch, Wolf, JennAir, and Gaggenau all offer steam. This is an education sale — most customers don't know what a steam oven does until you show them. Key demo: steam-reheat a piece of pizza. It comes out like fresh. Microwave-reheat the same pizza. Night and day difference. That's your demo.

**Combi Oven (Combination Steam + Convection).** The most versatile oven you can sell. Combines steam, convection, and sometimes microwave in one unit. Can do everything: steam vegetables, bake bread with steam injection (bakery-quality crust), roast a chicken with convection, reheat with steam. Miele, Wolf, Thermador, Gaggenau. Price: $3,500–$7,000. This is the oven for the serious cook who wants one appliance that does everything.

**Speed Oven.** Combines convection and microwave — cooks up to 4x faster than a conventional oven. Replaces the over-the-range microwave with something that actually cooks well. Miele, Wolf, JennAir, Thermador, Bosch, KitchenAid. Often installed as the upper unit in a double wall oven stack. The pitch: 'You get a real oven and a microwave in the same space, and it cooks faster than either one alone.'

**Microwave.** Over-the-range (OTR) — includes ventilation, saves counter space, most popular. Countertop — portable, no installation. Built-in/drawer — clean look, installed in cabinetry. Microwave drawers (Sharp, KitchenAid, Bosch) are popular in island installations and ADA-accessible kitchens.

sections.title: Cooktops: The Standalone Surface
content: **Gas Cooktop.** 30" (4 burners) or 36" (5–6 burners). Sealed burners are standard — easier to clean than open burners. Continuous cast-iron grates let you slide pots across burners. Premium cooktops offer brass burners (better heat distribution), simmer burners (low BTU for sauces), and wok rings.
**Electric Cooktop.** Radiant glass-ceramic. Clean, flat, affordable. Bridge elements (connect two burners into one long zone) are available on premium models for griddles and large pans.

**Induction Cooktop.** The future of cooking. 30" or 36". Flex zones (cook anywhere on the surface — Thermador Liberty, Bosch FlexInduction) are the premium feature. The cookware compatibility question always comes up — have a magnet on the floor. If it sticks to the pan, it works on induction. Most customers' existing cookware is already compatible.

**Downdraft Cooktop.** Built-in ventilation that rises from behind the cooktop or pulls air down through the surface. For island installations where overhead ventilation isn't possible. GE Profile, JennAir, KitchenAid. Less effective than overhead hoods but solves a real problem in open kitchens.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
content: Demo induction every single day to at least one customer. The boil test converts skeptics. Know the difference between freestanding and slide-in and be ready to show both side by side on the floor. A customer who walks in for a freestanding range and walks out with a slide-in range just spent $400–$800 more because you showed them the difference.
